body:
Language and script are different concepts

A language is a system of communication with its own vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation. A script is a system of written symbols used to represent a language.

Gujarati existed as a spoken and literary language before the modern Gujarati script became the dominant system for writing it. The historical development of Gujarati as a language must therefore be distinguished from the development of its script.

Origin of the Gujarati script

The Gujarati script belongs to the Brahmi-derived family of Indian scripts. It developed from the northern Indian Nagari writing tradition and is closely related to Devanagari.

Earlier forms of Nagari writing retained a horizontal line above the characters. In the commercial and informal writing traditions of western India, letter shapes gradually became more simplified, and the horizontal headline was omitted.

The resulting script became particularly useful for account keeping, commercial records and correspondence. Its historical commercial form was associated with names such as Sarafi, meaning bankers' writing, and Mahajani, associated with merchants.

The term Mahajani can also refer more broadly to historical mercantile writing systems used in northern and western India. It should not be assumed that every historical script called Mahajani was identical to modern Gujarati script.

A document dated 1592 CE is commonly cited as early surviving evidence of the distinctive Gujarati characters. This is evidence of documented usage, not an exact date for the invention of the script.

The absence of Shirorekha

The most easily recognisable difference between Gujarati and Devanagari is the absence of the Shirorekha in Gujarati.

Shirorekha refers to the horizontal headline typically present above Devanagari letters and often connecting the characters of a word. Modern Gujarati letter forms generally lack this connecting headline.

Despite this visible difference, the 2 scripts share many structural characteristics because of their related historical origins.

Basic characteristics of Gujarati writing

Gujarati is written from left to right and is classified as an abugida, also called an alphasyllabary.

In an abugida, a basic consonant character normally contains an inherent vowel. The writer can modify or suppress that vowel by adding appropriate signs.

  • Independent vowels: Used when a vowel stands independently, such as at the beginning of a syllable without a preceding consonant.
  • Dependent vowel signs: Attached to consonant characters to indicate a different vowel.
  • Virama: A sign used to suppress the inherent vowel. In Gujarati, it is commonly called Khodo or Khodo Halant.
  • Conjunct consonants: Combinations of consonants that represent consonant clusters.

These features are shared with other Brahmi-derived scripts. The absence of Shirorekha does not mean that Gujarati has a fundamentally different writing system from Devanagari.

Historical and modern functions

Script or writing traditionAssociation with Gujarati
BrahmiHistorical ancestor of the script family
Nagari and DevanagariClosely related historical writing traditions
Sarafi and Mahajani traditionsHistorical banking and commercial writing
Modern Gujarati scriptBooks, newspapers, education, public communication and digital writing

The expansion of printing during the 19th century helped establish the modern Gujarati script in education, literature and public communication.

Prelims focus

  • The Gujarati script belongs to the Brahmi-derived script family.
  • It is closely related to the Nagari and Devanagari traditions.
  • Gujarati script generally lacks Shirorekha.
  • It is written from left to right.
  • Its writing system is an abugida.
  • Trap: The origin of the Gujarati language and the origin of its script are separate historical questions.

[References: The Unicode Standard, Version 16.0, Chapter 12, Section 12.4.1, Gujarati; Neo-Brahmi Generation Panel, Proposal for a Gujarati Script Root Zone Label Generation Ruleset, 6 March 2019, Section 3.1, The Evolution of the Script, p. 3; The Written Languages of the World: A Survey of the Degree and Modes of Use, Vol. 2, India, Book 1, Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, 1989, Gujarati section; Unicode Demystified, Chapter 9, Gujarati section, drawing on P. J. Mistry's study of Gujarati writing. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Gujarati Script: Origin, Characteristics and Historical Usage

body:
Meaning of a regional dialect

A dialect is a variety of a language distinguished by characteristic pronunciation, vocabulary or grammatical usage. A regional dialect develops when a speech community acquires linguistic features associated with a particular geographical area.

Gujarati exhibits considerable regional variation. People from different parts of Gujarat can generally recognise differences in speech even when they understand one another.

Geographical separation, historical patterns of settlement, local communities, migration and contact with neighbouring languages contribute to this variation.

The 4 principal regional dialect groups

A widely used geographical classification identifies 4 major regional groups of Gujarati: North Gujarati, Central Gujarati, South Gujarati and the Gujarati varieties of Saurashtra.

Pattani or North Gujarati

Pattani, also spelled Patani, is associated with northern Gujarat, particularly Patan and the adjoining areas of Mehsana and Banaskantha.

It differs from Standard Gujarati in several pronunciation patterns and regional expressions. For example, pronunciations represented in transliteration as gom and kom may occur in place of the standard forms gam and kam, meaning village and work respectively.

The name Pattani is associated with Patan, an important historical centre of Gujarat.

Charotari or Central Gujarati

Charotari is associated especially with the Charotar region of central Gujarat, including Anand and Kheda. The wider central Gujarati speech region also includes important varieties associated with Ahmedabad and Vadodara.

The central Gujarati speech tradition has a close historical relationship with the development of Standard Gujarati. However, local Charotari speech is not necessarily identical in every respect to the standard written language.

Surati or South Gujarati

Surati, also spelled Surti, is associated with Surat and the surrounding areas of southern Gujarat, including parts of Navsari and adjoining regions.

It possesses distinctive patterns of pronunciation, vocabulary and speech rhythm. The commercial history of Surat and the interaction of different communities in southern Gujarat have contributed to the linguistic diversity of this region.

The speech of southern Gujarat also varies between localities and communities. Surati should therefore be understood as a major regional variety rather than a single completely uniform form of speech.

Kathiawadi or Saurashtri Gujarati

Kathiawadi is the broad regional designation for Gujarati varieties spoken in the Saurashtra peninsula, historically known as Kathiawar.

It differs from mainland Gujarati in pronunciation, expressions and certain grammatical forms. Some regional forms also preserve features that have changed in the standard language.

Saurashtra contains several distinct local varieties. Therefore, the term Kathiawadi includes a group of related dialects rather than one uniform variety.

Important subdivisions of Kathiawadi

SubdialectTraditional regional associationRepresentative places
HalariHalarJamnagar and parts of Rajkot
SorathiSorathJunagadh and adjoining areas
GohilwadiGohilwadBhavnagar and parts of Amreli
Zalawadi or JhalawadiZalawadSurendranagar region

These subdialect names reflect historical and cultural regions of Saurashtra. Their geographical distribution does not necessarily follow the exact boundaries of present-day administrative districts.

Dialect boundaries are not fixed

Regional speech changes gradually across geographical areas. Migration and contact between communities create transitional varieties. A district can contain speakers of more than one dialect, and the same dialect may extend across several districts.

Dialect and accent

An accent primarily concerns pronunciation. A dialect may differ from another variety in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar. Thus, a difference in accent is one possible feature of dialect variation, but dialect is the broader concept.

Prelims focus

  • Pattani: North Gujarat, particularly the Patan region.
  • Charotari: Central Gujarat, particularly Anand and Kheda.
  • Surati: South Gujarat, particularly Surat.
  • Kathiawadi: Saurashtra peninsula.
  • Halari, Sorathi, Gohilwadi and Zalawadi are associated with Saurashtra.
  • Trap: Gujarati dialect regions do not coincide exactly with district boundaries.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Dialect and Gujarati Dialects, sections on the 4 principal regional varieties; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Gujarati Language and Literature, sections on Saurashtra and its subdialects; Central Institute of Indian Languages, Linguistic Data Consortium for Indian Languages, Gujarati Raw Speech Corpus, Description and Overview; George Cardona, A Gujarati Reference Grammar, Introduction; Central Institute of Indian Languages, Hindi-English-Gujarati Trilingual Dictionary, 2017, introductory description; People's Linguistic Survey of India, The Languages of Gujarat, Diu & Daman and Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Vol. 9, Part 2, Section I. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Major Regional Dialects of Gujarati

body:
Language spoken in Gujarat does not necessarily mean a dialect of Gujarati

Gujarat is a multilingual state. Alongside the regional and social varieties of Gujarati, several other languages and speech traditions are spoken by communities within the state.

A geographical location alone cannot determine the linguistic classification of a speech form. Classification also depends on historical ancestry, grammatical structure, vocabulary, relationships with neighbouring languages and the identity of its speakers.

Kachchhi

Kachchhi, also spelled Kutchi or Kutchhi, is the speech tradition particularly associated with the Kachchh region of Gujarat.

Kachchhi has close linguistic affinities with Sindhi and has also been influenced by Gujarati and neighbouring western Indian speech varieties. It is therefore significant in understanding the linguistic connections between Gujarat and the adjoining Sindh region.

Although Kachchhi is sometimes grouped with Gujarati in broad descriptions of Gujarat's regional speech, it is not simply another name for Standard Gujarati or Kathiawadi.

The 2011 Census of India grouped Kachchhi under the language category of Sindhi in its mother-tongue tables. This is a census classification for the 2011 enumeration and should not be treated as the only possible linguistic classification of Kachchhi.

Gujarati script is also used to write Kachchhi. The use of a common script does not establish that 2 speech varieties are the same language.

Kachchhi is associated geographically with Gujarat but has close linguistic affinities with Sindhi. The regional classification of a speech community and the linguistic classification of its language are different matters.

Tribal languages of Gujarat

The eastern and southern regions of Gujarat contain several distinct tribal linguistic traditions. These form an important part of the state's cultural and linguistic heritage.

Language or speech varietyBroad geographical association
Bhili varietiesEastern and northeastern tribal regions of Gujarat
RathwiEastern Gujarat, particularly the Chhota Udepur region
GamitSouthern Gujarat, including the Tapi region
ChaudhariSouthern Gujarat
DhodiaSouthern Gujarat, including areas around Valsad and Navsari
DangiThe Dang region
Konkana or KuknaSouthern Gujarat and neighbouring areas

These languages and varieties have experienced varying degrees of interaction with Gujarati, Marathi, Bhili and other neighbouring linguistic traditions. They possess their own regional or community identities and should not all be described indiscriminately as Gujarati dialects.

Census classification and linguistic classification

A population census groups reported mother tongues into broader language categories for statistical presentation. These categories are useful for interpreting official demographic information, but they do not necessarily settle every scholarly question about the relationship between a language and its dialects.

In the Gujarat mother-tongue table of Census 2011, Pattani and Saurashtra or Saurashtri appear under Gujarati, while Kachchhi appears under Sindhi. Several tribal mother tongues, including Gamti or Gavit, Chodhari and Dhodia, are grouped under the broader Bhili or Bhilodi category in the census classification.

The People's Linguistic Survey of India, by contrast, gives separate attention to numerous community languages and varieties, including Kachchhi, Gamit, Rathwi, Dhodia and Dangi. This approach makes their individual linguistic and cultural identities more visible.

The classification used in an examination statement must be identified before comparing language groups. A census category, a geographical designation and a linguistic classification do not always have identical boundaries.

Prelims focus

  • Kachchhi is principally associated with Kachchh.
  • Kachchhi has close linguistic affinities with Sindhi.
  • Census 2011 grouped Kachchhi under Sindhi.
  • Gamit and Chaudhari are associated with southern Gujarat.
  • Dangi is associated with the Dang region.
  • Trap: All languages spoken within Gujarat are not necessarily dialects of Gujarati.

[References: Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, Census 2011, Table C-16, Population by Mother Tongue, Gujarat, reference PC11_C16-24; People's Linguistic Survey of India, The Languages of Gujarat, Diu & Daman and Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Vol. 9, Part 2, Sections II and III; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Gujarati Language and Literature, discussion of Kachchhi and tribal speech varieties; Unicode Demystified, Chapter 9, Gujarati section. Census classification relates specifically to the 2011 enumeration. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
